screens.title: Holistic Solution Architecture with Red Hat
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we lift your view from individual components to entire ecosystems built with Red Hat technologies. You will learn how to translate business needs and non-functional requirements into a cohesive architecture that combines RHEL, OpenShift, Ansible Automation Platform, Ceph Storage, Satellite, IdM, and virtualization or cloud components. We’ll show how these products act together across the lifecycle: design, deploy, operate, scale, and retire. A practical example will guide you through modernizing legacy applications while introducing cloud-native services, and you will see why automation-first thinking and lifecycle management reduce operational risk. Pay attention to common architectural pitfalls we highlight, like treating product features in isolation or designing only for peak capacity. By the end you should be able to produce a high-level hybrid-cloud platform outline, justify each Red Hat component by NFRs, and call out the automation and identity controls that keep the environment secure and manageable. Think about a real application your organization runs and how these principles would change how that application is deployed and operated.

Third, you will apply common architectural design patterns—such as high availability and load distribution—to meet enterprise constraints. Fourth, you will develop a strategic mindset to weigh product trade-offs against business goals and team capabilities. screens.title: Holistic Architecture — definition and scope
screens.narratorSegment: Holistic architecture is a comprehensive approach that treats a solution as an interconnected system rather than a collection of independent products. In a Red Hat context, that means understanding RHEL, OpenShift, Ansible, Ceph, Satellite, IdM, and virtualization components as parts of a single operational surface with shared lifecycle concerns. Practically, holistic design demands early consideration of non-functional requirements—security, performance, availability, and compliance—and then mapping those requirements to product responsibilities. For example, encryption at rest maps to storage choices like Ceph, while automated patching maps to Satellite and Ansible. A useful concrete example is modernizing a legacy Java application: you decide whether to containerize it for OpenShift or run it on managed RHEL virtual machines; that decision depends on desired scalability and compatibility constraints. A common misconception is that assembling products with point-to-point scripts is sufficient. In truth, without lifecycle automation and global identity integration, operational toil and security gaps emerge. The core takeaway is to align product roles to NFRs and build automation and lifecycle processes from day one. Ask yourself: which NFR would fail first if automation or identity integration were missing?

content.html:
Module 12›Chapter 12.1›Holistic Architecture
Holistic Architecture — definition and scope
Understand scope, responsibilities, and lifecycle obligations across the Red Hat portfolio.
Definition
A system-level design approach that maps NFRs to product roles and plans for the entire lifecycle, from deployment to retirement.
Concrete example
Modernize a legacy Java app: decide between containerizing for OpenShift or running on RHEL VMs based on scalability, compatibility, and team skill set.
Key points
  • Map each NFR to a product responsibility and a lifecycle action.
  • Plan automation and identity integration early to avoid operational gaps.
  • Design for typical loads and scale patterns, not only rare peaks.
Misconception
Point solutions equal architecture — false. Integration and lifecycle are required.
Pro tip
Capture NFRs in a short table and map them to product choices before diving into diagrams.

screens.title: From Business Requirements to Product Mapping
screens.narratorSegment: Start every architecture by documenting business requirements and non-functional requirements. This simple step keeps technical choices aligned with outcomes. The process we use has four clear stages: capture requirements, rank NFRs, map to product responsibilities, and design integration and automation. Capture means interviewing stakeholders to learn expected availability, compliance needs, performance targets, and operational constraints. Ranking forces trade-off decisions—if budget is tight, you may prioritize availability differently than if regulatory compliance is strict. Mapping translates NFRs to products: OpenShift for rapid scaling and developer workflows, Ceph for scalable persistent storage, Satellite for patching and content delivery, IdM for centralized identity, and Ansible for automation across those systems. Integration design specifies identity flows, storage attachments, network segmentation, and automation orchestration. A concrete example: if compliance requires centralized auditing and role separation, IdM plus OpenShift RBAC and Satellite-managed patching become mandatory parts of the map. A common pitfall is skipping ranking and ending up with incompatible or over-engineered solutions. The closing question: which requirement would you rank highest for your busiest application, and how would that choice narrow your product set? From Business Requirements to Product Mapping means use a simple capture → rank → map → integrate process to turn nfrs into concrete red hat product roles.. In practical terms, a repeatable process to match nfrs with red hat capabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12›Chapter 12.1›Requirements → Mapping
Process: Capture → Rank → Map → Integrate
Follow these steps to avoid mismatched product selection.
1. Capture
Interview stakeholders to gather availability, compliance, performance, and operational constraints.
2. Rank
Prioritize NFRs so trade-offs are explicit before product selection.
3. Map
Assign responsibilities to RHEL, OpenShift, Ceph, Satellite, IdM, and Ansible based on NFRs.
4. Integrate
Design identity, storage, network, and automation interactions and define lifecycle tasks.
Example scenario
A regulated finance app needs 99.99% availability and encrypted storage. Rank availability and encryption highest, then map to product choices: OpenShift for HA and automatic scaling, Ceph for encrypted persistent volumes, Satellite for consistent patching, IdM for centralized access control, and Ansible to automate deployment and compliance checks.
Common mistake
Selecting products before ranking NFRs, which can lead to expensive refactors.
Check your understanding
List three NFRs for a public-facing storefront and map one product to each.

screens.title: RHEL as the foundational layer
screens.narratorSegment: RHEL plays a foundational role: it is the consistent operating system across physical servers, virtual machines, and cloud instances. That consistency reduces variability in behavior and security posture, and it simplifies lifecycle actions like patching, compliance checks, and configuration management. For example, using Satellite for content delivery and patching assumes a uniform RHEL baseline so updates behave predictably. When architects choose where to run an application, that decision must account for the OS baseline: a legacy application that requires specific OS libraries might be easier to keep on RHEL VMs, while a cloud-native microservice should target OpenShift but still depend on consistent RHEL nodes for platform services. A common misconception is that containers remove the need for a uniform OS. While containers package application dependencies, cluster nodes and operators still rely on a secure, patched OS image. The concrete takeaway: choose RHEL deliberately as the ground truth for security, compliance, and predictable operations, and plan lifecycle tooling around it. Which part of your environment would break first if node OS updates were inconsistent? RHEL as the foundational layer means rhel provides a predictable, manageable base for platform services, patching, and compliance across deployment targets.. In practical terms, why a consistent os matters across physical, virtual, and cloud. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12›Chapter 12.1›RHEL Foundation
RHEL as the foundational layer
Use a consistent OS to simplify patching, compliance, and predictable behavior across environments.
  • Uniform OS images reduce unexpected runtime differences.
  • Satellite and Ansible rely on consistent OS baselines for content and automation.
  • Choose RHEL where security and long-term support are required.
Example and implications
A legacy database requiring OS-level libraries is safer on a managed RHEL VM, while services suited for containers run on OpenShift but depend on RHEL nodes for the control plane and operators. Inconsistent OS updates cause nodes to drift and can break platform services.
Misconception
Containers mean OS uniformity is irrelevant — false. Node-level consistency still matters for reliability and security.
Pro tip
Define a single supported OS image catalogue and automate node builds with Ansible for repeatability.

screens.title: OpenShift for cloud-native and modernization
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift is the platform of choice when requirements emphasize rapid deployment, developer workflows, and automatic scaling. It provides orchestration, built-in high availability, and platform security controls that ease the operational burden of running microservices at scale. When modernizing legacy applications, one approach is to containerize them and run them on OpenShift to gain improved scaling and deployment velocity. Alternatively, some legacy workloads may remain on RHEL VMs if containerization would introduce unacceptable compatibility risk. A concrete example: a customer moves stateless web front-ends to OpenShift to leverage horizontal autoscaling, while keeping a monolithic transactional backend on RHEL VMs during a phased migration. A common pitfall is deploying OpenShift without integrating lifecycle and patching strategies; without Satellite and Ansible in the plan, clusters and nodes can drift and create security gaps. The key insight is to align deployment patterns to the application’s NFRs and ensure the platform’s lifecycle tools are part of the architecture from the start. OpenShift for cloud-native and modernization means openshift accelerates cloud-native development and scaling, but must be integrated with lifecycle and identity systems to avoid operational drift.. In practical terms, using openshift to host new services and modernize existing apps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12›Chapter 12.1›OpenShift Role
OpenShift for cloud-native and modernization
Use OpenShift for developer velocity, autoscaling, and platform-level security.
  • Hosts containers and provides orchestration, HA, and developer workflows.
  • Supports phased migration: containerize stateless components first.
  • Requires lifecycle integration to avoid drift.
Scenario
Migrate a web front-end to OpenShift for autoscaling while retaining a core transactional system on RHEL VMs until compatibility is validated. Use Ansible to automate deployment pipelines and Satellite for node-level OS updates.
Common mistake
Assuming OpenShift eliminates the need for OS and patch management — it does not.
Checkpoint
Identify which parts of your app benefit most from containerization and which require VM continuity.

screens.title: Ansible Automation Platform — the glue
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible Automation Platform acts as the automation backbone. It automates repetitive operations: provisioning RHEL systems, deploying applications to OpenShift, configuring Ceph storage, updating Satellite content views, and enforcing security policies. Its importance is that automation turns design decisions into reproducible, testable runbooks, and reduces manual steps that cause configuration drift. A concrete example is a playbook that provisions a set of RHEL nodes, registers them with Satellite, enrolls them in IdM, and deploys container runtime prerequisites for OpenShift. That single automation flow reduces time-to-deploy and enforces consistency. A common misconception is treating automation as a later convenience; in practice, automation must be designed alongside the architecture because it becomes the operational contract for the system. The takeaway: treat Ansible playbooks and automation pipelines as first-class artifacts of your architecture, version them, test them, and include them in lifecycle planning. Ansible Automation Platform — the glue means ansible converts architecture decisions into repeatable, tested processes that prevent drift and accelerate operations.. In practical terms, automating provisioning, configuration, and enforcement across the stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12›Chapter 12.1›Ansible Automation
Ansible Automation Platform — the glue
Use automation to make provisioning, configuration, and policy enforcement repeatable and auditable.
  • Automate provisioning of RHEL nodes and registration with Satellite and IdM.
  • Deploy applications and infrastructure configuration to OpenShift and VMs.
  • Use automation artifacts as versioned architecture contracts.
Concrete example
A playbook sequence creates RHEL nodes, registers them with Satellite, applies security hardening, integrates them into IdM groups, and then deploys container runtime settings required by OpenShift, all in a repeatable pipeline.
Misconception
Automation is optional — it is not. Without it, scaling and compliance become manual, error-prone tasks.
Pro tip
Keep automation declarative, test playbooks in staging, and treat playbooks as part of your architecture repository.

screens.title: Satellite and Lifecycle Management
screens.narratorSegment: Satellite provides centralized content delivery, patching, and lifecycle management for RHEL systems. In an enterprise architecture, Satellite reduces the operational burden of keeping hundreds or thousands of nodes consistent and compliant. For example, you can create content views and staged deployments so updates are tested before wide release. Satellite integrates with Ansible to apply configuration changes and with IdM to control which groups receive updates. A common mistake is to rely on ad-hoc updating or manual SSH sessions for patching; that approach doesn't scale and increases risk. A concrete scenario is a cluster upgrade: Satellite stages OS updates to a small test cohort, Ansible runs validation checks, then Satellite rolls the update across the fleet. The key point is to include Satellite-based lifecycle workflows in your architecture up front, because patching and content management are continuous activities that shape operational processes and downtime windows. Satellite and Lifecycle Management means include satellite-managed content and staged updates as part of architecture to maintain compliance and reduce risk.. In practical terms, managing content, patches, and system lifecycle at scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12›Chapter 12.1›Satellite & Lifecycle
Satellite and Lifecycle Management
Use Satellite to stage updates, deliver content, and manage system lifecycles at scale.
  • Create content views for controlled rollouts.
  • Integrate lifecycle actions with Ansible for validation and remediation.
  • Plan update windows and rollback procedures in architecture designs.
Example workflow
Stage OS updates to a test cohort in Satellite, run Ansible validation playbooks, and then release the content view to production with rollback tested ahead of time.
Common mistake
Treating patching as ad-hoc; it must be an integral, repeatable process in the architecture.
Pro tip
Define and document content view promotion criteria before automating rollouts.

screens.title: Red Hat Ceph Storage for unified persistence
screens.narratorSegment: Red Hat Ceph Storage offers a unified, scalable storage platform capable of block, file, and object services. In a hybrid Red Hat architecture, Ceph can provide persistent volumes to OpenShift, backing for OpenStack instances, and shared storage for traditional workloads. The value is a single storage layer that reduces fragmentation and simplifies data management and policies like encryption at rest. A practical example: OpenShift persistent volumes use Ceph RBD for highly available block storage; OpenStack instances use Ceph for instance disks; and Ceph Object storage can serve backups or expensive archival data. A common misconception is to pick storage solely by cost per terabyte; instead, align storage features with performance, durability, and encryption NFRs. Also plan for recovery and replication strategies at design time to avoid single points of failure. In this lesson we lift your view from individual components to entire ecosystems built with Red Hat technologies. You will learn how to translate business needs and non-functional requirements into a cohesive architecture that combines RHEL, OpenShift, Ansible Automation Platform, Ceph Storage, Satellite, IdM, and virtualization or cloud components. We’ll show how these products act together across the lifecycle: design, deploy, operate, scale, and retire. A practical example will guide you through modernizing legacy applications while introducing cloud-native services, and you will see why automation-first thinking and lifecycle management reduce operational risk. Pay attention to common architectural pitfalls we highlight, like treating product features in isolation or designing only for peak capacity. By the end you should be able to produce a high-level hybrid-cloud platform outline, justify each Red Hat component by NFRs, and call out the automation and identity controls that keep the environment secure and manageable. Think about a real application your organization runs and how these principles would change how that application is deployed and operated.

These objectives focus on the skills you need as an architect working with Red Hat technologies. First, you will understand core principles of holistic solution architecture: how components interact, where lifecycle concerns appear, and how automation changes operational risk. Second, you will be able to identify key Red Hat products and clearly state their roles in multi-tier solutions, mapping each product to concrete non-functional needs like security, availability, and performance. Third, you will apply common architectural design patterns—such as high availability and load distribution—to meet enterprise constraints. Fourth, you will develop a strategic mindset to weigh product trade-offs against business goals and team capabilities. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the skill, and a verified competency milestone to indicate readiness. As you work through the lessons, try to map real requirements you know to the product roles we discuss. That practice turns abstract knowledge into practical architecture fluency.

Holistic architecture is a comprehensive approach that treats a solution as an interconnected system rather than a collection of independent products. In a Red Hat context, that means understanding RHEL, OpenShift, Ansible, Ceph, Satellite, IdM, and virtualization components as parts of a single operational surface with shared lifecycle concerns. Practically, holistic design demands early consideration of non-functional requirements—security, performance, availability, and compliance—and then mapping those requirements to product responsibilities. For example, encryption at rest maps to storage choices like Ceph, while automated patching maps to Satellite and Ansible. A useful concrete example is modernizing a legacy Java application: you decide whether to containerize it for OpenShift or run it on managed RHEL virtual machines; that decision depends on desired scalability and compatibility constraints. A common misconception is that assembling products with point-to-point scripts is sufficient. The core takeaway is to align product roles to NFRs and build automation and lifecycle processes from day one. Ask yourself: which NFR would fail first if automation or identity integration were missing?

Keep on RHEL VMs when deep OS integration, legacy dependencies, or regulatory isolation make containerization risky.
